en: In the personalized offers regime, Riot describes the feature as dependent on gameplay traces processed through comparison and profiling, without the complete selection criteria becoming publicly auditable. When explaining why skins appear for champions the player does not use often, official support states that “DescontoBot uses your player history from the last six months to compare you to other players with similar patterns and create offers you will like” and adds that “its analysis is not made only with the Champions you use most” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2023b)</2>. This kind of formulation is methodologically valuable because it shows, at the same time, the measurable base mobilized by the service and the preservation of opacity regarding the recommendation criteria, reinforcing that governance by architecture can operate as the administration of probabilities and of attention, and not as a simple display of options in a shop window. <3>↩</3>

The contractual authorization for continuous modification of the enjoyment environment itself appears explicitly in the clause on updates and modifications. The relevance of the passage lies not in an abstract power to “change the game”, but in revealing that the technical architecture that distributes visibility, organizes flows and enables consumption is not a scenery external to the bond. It is part of the service itself and can be reconfigured as an ordinary technique for governing the experience. <1>↩</1>

Perttu Jalovaara is a researcher at <1>Aalto University School of Science</1>, where he developed, in the context of the <2>Master’s </2> <3>Programme in Mathematics and Operations Researc</3>h, a dissertation on estimating win probability in <4>esports</4>, with a specific focus on <5>League of Legends </5><6>Jalovaara</6><7>(Jalovaara, 2024, p. 3)</7>. His work belongs to the field of <8>esports analytics</8> and is useful, at this point, for offering a quantitative and methodologically rigorous treatment of problems of reading performance, context and strategic decision in a digital competitive environment, especially by demonstrating the insufficiency of simple aggregate statistics and the need for analytical contextualization of the game's variables <9>Jalovaara</9><10>(Jalovaara, 2024, p. 7)</10>. <11>↩</11>

The reorganization of immaterial consumption around governed ecosystems makes it insufficient to treat the conflict as a simple contractual divergence or as a fluctuation of individual preferences. The enjoyment that sustains the value of the IOC depends on an administered environment in which visibility, reputation, access, permanence and sanction are distributed according to internal criteria, by predominantly architectural and informational means. When the practical shaping of the object is produced by design, protocols, curation and technical <1>enforcement</1>, vulnerability ceases to be exhausted in occasional information deficits and takes on institutional density, since the asymmetry resides in the concentrated control of the variables that make the experience legible, commensurable and continuable over time, without proportional guarantees of intelligible publicity, verification and contestation. The question, then, is to situate this kind of private power within a tradition of legal reconstruction oriented by material changes in the conditions of social life, without depending on equating the platform with the figure of the State.

In their article, Warren and Brandeis<1><2>380</2></1> ([201-?]) argue that recent inventions and expanding business practices intensified forms of intrusion that the legal order, if it remains tied to earlier schemes, cannot adequately capture. From there, the authors defend the recognition of a right to privacy as a legitimate right <3>p. 348</3> to be let alone, distinguishing it from adjacent institutes that protect different interests, such as defamation, aimed at reputation before third parties, and literary/authorial property, aimed at the economic exploitation of publication. The text also sets out cautions and limitations, especially in situations of public interest and of exposure inherent to certain functions, and indicates legal remedies compatible with the structure of<4> tort law</4>, including damages and injunctive relief. The central gain lies in establishing a legitimate argumentative precedent. When the technical environment reorganizes vulnerability at scale, legal reconstruction is not moralism, but a necessary response to keep the effects of new forms of power and intrusion controllable in institutional terms.

The recourse to Warren and Brandeis does not operate by thematic identity, but by homology of situation. Technical change structurally alters the conditions of exposure, harm and vulnerability, and demands an adjustment of categories so that protection remains adherent to the real mode of production of the conflict. This does not imply equating platform with State nor constitutionalizing every private dispute, but recognizing that certain private powers, when exercised through architecture, information and enforcement at scale, generate asymmetries and risks that are not exhausted in contractual literalness. If reconstruction was necessary when techniques and business models reconfigured patterns of exposure and protection at the end of the nineteenth century, the same rationality justifies describing vulnerabilities produced by contemporary digital infrastructures in terms that allow legal control without resorting to simplifying fictions about market neutrality or about the sufficiency of formal will.

The structural orientation of this method becomes even clearer when the article shifts the problem from the sphere of individual vice to the social and economic machinery that makes intrusion reproducible at scale. The relevant critique is not organized as the reproach of an isolated agent, but as the diagnosis of an activity that becomes institutionalized as commerce and starts operating by its own logic. Warren and Brandeis describe the invasion of private life as an industry, pursued with method and effrontery, in which the mercantile dynamic reproduces itself by feedback, since supply itself manufactures demand<1><2>381</2></1> <3>Brandeis</3><4>(Warren; Brandeis, [201-?], [p. 4])</4>.

<1>p. 349</1> By stating harm as the effect of a productive mechanism and of a circuit of manufactured demand, the text reinforces the idea that the adequate legal response is not moralization, but the reinterpretation of categories to make controllable a form of power whose operation is stabilized by technique, scale and business method. The consequence that matters here is that the focus falls on operating conditions and on the institutional organization of harm, opening room to recognize, in other environments of private governance, vulnerability produced by structure, and not by personal failure of the regulated subject.

Transposing this model to the IOC regime requires keeping the focus on the kind of power described. The core of the problem lies not in occasional breaches, but in a private infrastructure of practical governance capable of organizing, at scale, conditions of participation and enjoyment. In this environment, visibility and reputation function as economically relevant dimensions, internal rules are mutable, expectations are calibrated by curation and temporalization of the offer, and sanctions or functional restrictions may degrade the acquired position and reconfigure the economic meaning of enjoyment.

The relevant asymmetry stems from the concentrated control of the criteria that govern recognition, permanence and sanction, so that the consumer bears the effects without proportional access to the parameters that produce them. Once this kind of power is identified, it becomes justifiable to demand a legal language capable of following material changes in the conditions of enjoyment and vulnerability, without reducing the conflict to the literalness of the contract nor resorting to fictions about the neutrality of intermediation.

The prudence of the design proposed by Warren and Brandeis appears clearly in the section on limitations, in which the right to privacy is framed as calibrated protection, incapable of functioning as a general instrument of informational blocking. Public interest functions as a limit, since protection does not extend to publications whose content is of public <1>p. 350</1> or general interest, so as to preserve the circulation of information relevant to the community and to prevent privacy from becoming censorship <2>Brandeis</2><3>(Warren; Brandeis, [201-?], [p. 16])</3>.

Their work also sets limits by institutional context, recognizing that certain informational flows are part of the very functioning of institutions and, therefore, cannot be paralyzed by the new protection, as occurs with publications made in judicial proceedings and in legislative bodies, as well as in equivalent communications <1>Brandeis</1><2>(Warren; Brandeis, [201-?], [p. 19])</2>. The delimitation is completed by a criterion of proportionality associated with the means of propagation, admitting that, as a rule, there would be no redress for merely oral publication without special damage and that part of these occurrences must be tolerated to preserve freedom of expression, preventing the category from expanding to cover trivialities and preserving room for ordinary social practices without diffuse judicialization <3>Brandeis</3><4>(Warren; Brandeis, [201-?], [p. 19])</4>.

The methodological consequence of this calibration is that the limitation of power does not depend on its public nature, but on the way it stabilizes and on the effects it produces on conditions of life and participation. When practical normativity is exercised through mutable internal rules, access architecture and opaque informational intermediation, the relevant deficit is not the absence of a public-law label, but the absence of institutional reciprocity proportional to the dominion exercised over recognition, permanence and sanction.

It is in this strict sense that the expression “without authorization” operates as a descriptive category, since it names a power of social ordering that does not submit, to an equivalent extent, to minimum requirements of intelligible publicity of criteria, accessible reasoning, decisional coherence and effective avenues of contestation compatible with the economic and identity relevance of what is at stake. From this point on, the task ceases to be discussing whether the relationship is private or public and becomes identifying which instruments of control make the rationality of the exercise of this power examinable, which places the tradition of legal reconstruction in the face of material changes once again as a parameter for building proportional limits and duties without resorting to statist fictions.

The institutional framework proposed by Warren and Brandeis also rests on a diagnosis of civilization and modern life, in which the need for protection emerges as a response to collective pressures and not as a casuistic reaction to isolated episodes. The text associates the expansion of legally protected interests with the fact that civilizational advance intensified intellectual and emotional life and heightened sensibility, making it more evident that a decisive part of human experience is not concentrated in physical goods <1>Brandeis</1><2>(Warren; Brandeis, [201-?], [p. 3])</2>.

<1>p. 351</1> In continuation, privacy is described as a functional condition for bearing modernity, since the intensity and complexity of life make some form of retreat from the world necessary and, under the refining effect of culture, the individual becomes more sensitive to publicity, making solitude and privacy more essential <2>Brandeis</2><3>(Warren; Brandeis, [201-?], [p. 4])</3>. This allows protection to be treated as a mechanism of legal accommodation of new structural pressures, which reinforces the legitimacy of conceptual reconstructions when technical infrastructures and intermediation models reorganize, at scale, the conditions of exposure, enjoyment and vulnerability.

Once it is established that governance by architecture and by information constitutes a form of practical normativity capable of organizing access, visibility, permanence and sanction in environments of ecosystem-dependent enjoyment, the problem can no longer be stated as mere contractual friction and comes to demand a controllable language to describe limits and criteria of accountability compatible with the density of the dominion exercised. The contribution obtained situates the proposed shift within a tradition of legal reconstruction that responds to material changes in the conditions of social life, showing that, when techniques and business methods reorganize exposure and vulnerability at scale, the adequacy of categories is not voluntarism, but a condition of the institutional intelligibility of the conflict.

With this, it becomes possible to treat the asymmetry not as subjective discomfort, but as a structural deficit of proportional reciprocity, to be addressed by instruments that make the criteria, rationalities and impacts of the exercise of power inside the ecosystem examinable. This framework allows describing how governance produces adherence, self-adjustment and subjection through performance, comparison and the management of symbolic risk without individual moral attribution. With this, the position of enjoyment reveals itself also as a position of conformity and dependence, preparing the formulation of proportional duties and of parameters of transparency, stability and restoration adequate to the IOC regime.

Entitled <1>The Right to Privacy</1>, the seminal article by Samuel D. Warren and Louis D. Brandeis <2>([201-?])</2>, originally published by the <3>Harvard Law Review</3> in 1890, formulates a matrix of legal reconstruction in the face of technical and social mutations that alter conditions of exposure, vulnerability and harm. The text starts from the premise that the common law does not operate as a static system, but as a tradition capable of developing new protective contours when material changes reconfigure interests worthy of protection. Here, the interest of the argument is methodological and does not depend on institutional transplant between <4>common law</4> and <5>civil law,</5> since the point lies not in specific precedent techniques, but in the need to readjust legal categories when material transformation makes the available framework anachronistic. From this perspective, new technologies and new business models shift the boundary between the socially protected space and the sphere of subjection, and demand an adjustment of categories so that protection remains adherent to the real mode of production of the conflict. <6>↩</6>

Warren and Brandeis build <1>The Right to Privacy</1> as an institutional response to a material change in social life. The starting point is not a moral judgment about inconvenient individuals, but the perception that “Recent inventions and business methods call attention to the next step which must be taken for the protection of the person” <2>Brandeis</2><3>(Warren; Brandeis, [201-?], [p. 3])</3>. Technical modernity structurally alters the conditions of exposure and capture of everyday life, and the text describes this passage with images of concrete intrusion, stating that “Instantaneous photographs and newspaper enterprise have invaded the sacred precincts of private and domestic life” <4>Brandeis</4><5>(Warren; Brandeis, [201-?], [p. 3])</5>. The consequence is methodological, since inherited categories cease to capture the real mode of production of harm when technique and enterprise make intrusion reproducible at scale. In this key, the central critique shifts the focus from the “isolated agent” to the economic machinery that institutionalizes intrusion. The authors expressly state that “Gossip is no longer the resource of the idle and of the vicious, but has become a trade, which is pursued with industry as well as effrontery” and conclude, bluntly, that “In this, as in other branches of commerce, the supply creates the demand” <6>Brandeis</6><7>(Warren; Brandeis, [201-?])</7>. Intrusion then comes to operate as a market practice, guided by circulation incentives and by a cumulative logic, in which repetition creates social tolerance and lowers standards, since “Each crop of unseemly gossip, thus harvested, becomes the seed of more” <8>Brandeis</8><9>(Warren; Brandeis, [201-?], [p. 3])</9>. Harm, therefore, is not only the published episode, but the commercial circuit that manufactures appetite, normalizes exposure and expands vulnerability as a collective condition. It is from this diagnosis that the protective formulation emerges. The text proposes a protection that allows resisting intrusion without turning privacy into generalized censorship, articulating the right as “the right to be let alone” and, at the same time, setting limits and cautions, above all for public interest and for institutional contexts in which the circulation of information is functional <10>Brandeis</10><11>(Warren; Brandeis, [201-?], [p. 2])</11>. The strength of the article lies in its design. Protection is presented as a necessary legal reconstruction when technique and business methods shift boundaries of protection and make the previous framework anachronistic, without depending on moralization and without assuming that only state powers can produce structural asymmetries. <12>↩</12>

When governance by architecture and by information stabilizes as private administration of access, visibility, permanence and sanction, it produces a power that bears not only on occasional choices, but on the conditions of economic viability and social recognition inside the ecosystem. The enjoyment that sustains the value of the IOC depends on a legible and comparable position, and this position is preserved through adherence to criteria of recognition, update rhythms and performance standards instituted by the <1>p. 352</1> environment itself. Vulnerability is not exhausted in informational asymmetry or individual preferences, because permanence and belonging become governed resources, capable of producing self-adjustment, discipline and adherence as structural effects of the administered market.

The passage from the disciplinary model to a regime of performance allows contemporary subjection to be described without resorting to individual psychological analysis, since the axis of conformity ceases to depend on external prohibitions and starts operating through productive positivity and the internalization of demands. Byung-Chul Han<1><2>382</2></1> argues that the positivity of power can be more efficient than the negativity of duty, so that the achievement-subject tends to be faster and more productive than the obedience-subject, although this mutation does not erase discipline, since the achievement-subject remains disciplined and carries the disciplinary stage within it <3>Han</3><4>(Han, 2015, [p. 15])</4>. This shift helps to understand why environments governed by metrics, comparison and continuous incentive can produce stable self-adjustment without ostensive coercion, since freedom itself comes to function as a vehicle of demand. In this sense, Han describes the paradox by which freedom, when converted into a duty of unlimited performance, comes to produce coercion more efficiently than disciplinary obligation, which tends to meet limits <5>Han</5><6>(Han, 2017, [p. 8-9])</6>. The point is that adherence to the ecosystem can be produced as a structural effect, because preserving public commensurability and effective access to recognition requires continuous recalibration under criteria defined by the environment, converting performance and permanence into a practical condition of enjoyment.

In the IOC regime, recognition, visibility and permanence do not function as side effects of consumption, since they are part of the material conditions through which enjoyment becomes valuable and sustainable over time. The platform, by administering metrics, rankings, signals <1>p. 353</1> of prestige and forms of public comparison, establishes a grammar of performance that organizes what counts as success, adherence and regularity within the ecosystem. The result is functional convergence with the model described by Han.

Conformity does not depend on explicit command or frontal threat, because the environment itself makes discontinuity costly and misalignment risky, insofar as the loss of legibility, the drop in visibility and reputational downgrading directly affect the position of enjoyment that constitutes the relevant economic object. In this context, the consumer's adaptation does not express a personality trait, but a strategy of permanence in an administered market. Self-adjustment becomes rational under conditions in which value depends on preserving position in the ecosystem's internal hierarchies and on remaining eligible for validation and visibility, and the continuity of enjoyment comes to require keeping up with rhythms, expectations and standards defined by the infrastructure that controls access to the very criteria of recognition.

Adherence to the governed ecosystem need not be produced by frontal prohibition to acquire stability, because the regime of performance tends to convert freedom itself into an operator of conformity. Byung-Chul Han describes the contemporary subject as “lord and sovereign of itself”, freed from the external instance that would oblige it to work, and precisely for that reason placed in a situation in which the fall of the dominator does not lead to freedom, but makes “freedom and constraint coincide”, so that the subject “gives itself over to compulsive freedom” and to the “free constraint of maximizing performance” <1>Han</1><2>(Han, 2015, [p. 16])</2>. Here, the decisive mechanism is the one by which discipline comes to operate in the form of achievement, initiative and autonomy, making self-adjustment compatible with the feeling of choice, even when it is structured as an obligation to remain efficient and rewardable inside the environment.

The machinery becomes clearer when the governance of the ecosystem is described as the production of adherence through incentive, exposure and reward, and not as imposition by ostensive prohibition. Han argues that a smart power does not discipline the psyche through coercion or prohibition, but approaches it and summons it to participate and to share, exploiting freedom rather than denying it, precisely because it manages to operate without presenting itself as power <1>Han</1><2>(Han, 2017, [p. 18])</2>. The consequence is that subjection is not imposed as silence, but as continuous communication and exposure, and this active participation functions as a governance resource.

In <1>League of Legends</1>, this power that summons freedom to work in favor of conformity shows itself clearly in the ranked regime, because there performance is translated <2>p. 354</2> into position, and position becomes a public language of value. The competitive ladder organizes the experience as a comparable trajectory, in which the individual not only plays, but measures himself, ranks himself and makes himself available to the judgment of the ecosystem itself. This structure needs no direct coercion to produce discipline, since it converts initiative into a socially intelligible obligation. What is at stake is not a “game mode”, but the continuous production of a positional portrait that comes to operate as a summarized form of identity in that world.

This capture becomes even clearer when Riot itself describes the difference between MMR and rank as an institutional translation of the subject into numbers, so that the public ranking appears as a “relatable” representation of a calculated value that remains hidden. When explaining the system, official support states that MMR is secret and that rank exists as a mechanism to translate this MMR into a form that is accessible and progressive for the player <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2026h)</2>. The effect of this on the psychopolitics of performance is direct. The player's freedom is organized as a voluntary search for adequacy to the criterion that measures him, even when the criterion is opaque, because what becomes visible and socially legible is the positional result, and not the workings of the calculation.

For this reason, the ranked climb tends to transform leisure into a regime of rational self-exploitation. The platform administers symbolic risk through categories of progress, distribution and reclassification, including periodic structural changes that reposition the subject's value on the ladder and redefine the horizon of “climbing”, “holding” and “deserving” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2023d)</2><3><4>383</4></3>. Discipline, here, does not present itself as prohibition, but as a permanent summons to invest time, attention and performance so as not to lose public commensurability in the environment. The result is that conformity does not depend on an external order. It emerges as an internal need to preserve legibility, avoid falling and sustain a recognizable place in a hierarchy that the infrastructure itself produces and recalibrates over time.

This dependence, as with the other mechanisms of the ecosystem, is also not neutral from the standpoint of the contractual bond. The conditions of access and permanence are provided under a revocable and conditional license, and account termination implies loss of access to the <1>p. 355</1> environment and to associated data <2>Riot Games</2><3>(Riot Games, 2024e)</3><4><5>384</5></4>. Thus, the ranked ladder does not operate as detachable property. It operates as a grammar of recognition that only exists while the account and the service remain active, which makes leaving, slowing down or misalignment more costly than they would seem under an ontology of a static “product”.

Along these lines, contrasting the disciplinary panopticon with the digital panopticon, Han observes that the occupants of the new apparatus collaborate with its functioning through voluntary self-illumination and self-exposure <1>Han</1><2>(Han, 2017, [p. 13])</2>. The conclusion is that conformity can be produced as a structural effect of an ecosystem that mobilizes freedom, performance and exposure as a grammar of permanence, reducing the need for frontal coercion while intensifying the subject's dependence on the criteria that define recognition and value.

In <1>League of Legends</1>, psychopolitics manifests itself not only as an incentive to “do more”, but also as an inducement to “be the right way” if the goal is to remain eligible for the full experience of the ecosystem. The Honor system condenses this logic by turning conduct into a variable of administered reputation, whose practical consequence is not limited to a moral judgment, since it reorganizes rewards, privileges and access. Official support describes Honor as a general reflection of behavior “in and out of game”, stating that it “rewards” sportsmanlike conduct with benefits and “penalizes” inappropriate behavior with reduced rewards and restriction of communication privileges <2>Riot Games</2><3>(Riot Games, 2025a)</3><4><5>385</5></4>. Discipline, here, need not appear as an explicit threat, because it settles in as the subject's own everyday prudence. The player comes to manage himself to remain rewardable and socially legible, avoiding losses that are not only symbolic, but functional, insofar as they reach what can be accumulated, displayed and enjoyed in the continuity of enjoyment.

<1>p. 356</1> This shift of control to the inside of the subject becomes even clearer when the integrity policy itself connects punishments to material effects on progression and rewards. In a specific document on Honor restrictions, Riot describes that sanctions such as suspension and chat restriction lower the Honor level, lock progress and make the account ineligible for rewards tied to this regime <2>Riot Games</2><3>(Riot Games, 2017b)</3><4><5>386</5></4>. In this design, conformity is produced as self-preservation: it is not a matter of obeying out of abstract fear, but of avoiding a downgrade that alters the subject's position in the reward routines and in access to certain benefits, consolidating the idea that remaining “fit” is part of the consumption experience itself. Freedom, thus, operates as an operator of conformity because the subject anticipates the gaze of the ecosystem and adjusts his conduct so as not to lose eligibility.

This logic overflows the inside of the game and takes on the contours of identity governance, since the Terms of Service establish that the User Rules govern behavior during the game and also certain conduct outside the game, providing for disciplinary measures that may reach temporary suspension, account termination and even hardware banning <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2><3><4>387</4></3>. In addition, the contract makes explicit that the User Rules may apply to streams, recorded videos and social media posts, and admits the possibility of penalties applicable to multiple Riot services, including escalated across games <5>Riot Games</5><6>(Riot Games, 2024e)</6><7><8>388</8></7>. In this combination, what is observed is a regime in which the subject internalizes control as an obligation to remain eligible and acceptable before criteria that the ecosystem itself administers, extending the field of incidence of <9>p. 357</9> normativity beyond the strict moment of the match. The panopticon ceases to be only an exterior gaze because the individual comes to anticipate the sanction and to adjust his own behavior to remain within the borders of the rewardable, the communicable and the participable, as an ordinary condition of permanence.

Applied to the IOC regime, this machinery reveals that the ecosystem does not administer only access to content, but governs symbolic and positional risk as a condition of permanence. Value is not sustained as a static attribute of an acquired object, since it depends on continuity of enjoyment and on the preservation of public legibility within the ecosystem, so that losing visibility, temporal pertinence and belonging, or suffering positional downgrading produces economic effects that are not reducible to subjective inconvenience.

The platform, by controlling update rhythms, events, access windows, reputation scales and forms of comparison, converts permanence into a task and transforms keeping one's place into continuous work of monitoring and adjustment. In this context, the offer is not limited to delivering a one-off utility, because it organizes a circuit in which the very possibility of continuing to be “worth something” depends on adhering to parameters of performance and presence that the ecosystem naturalizes as a condition of participation.

The management of this risk functions as an instrument of discipline without needing to present itself as an explicit threat. Frequent return, constant attention and willingness to recalibrate conduct emerge as rational choices under conditions in which the cost of misalignment is the loss of commensurability and the erosion of accumulated symbolic capital, with a direct impact on the position of enjoyment that constitutes the economic core of the IOC.

The conversion of conduct into metrics is not limited to an external management technique, because it tends to reconfigure the way the subject perceives himself and stabilizes over time, shifting identity from a narrative structure to an additive structure of data. Byung-Chul Han formulates this contrast by arguing that the promise of self-knowledge through numbers fails at the most basic level, since the accumulation of records does not produce narrative, and a sense of self depends on giving an account of a trajectory, and not on adding up dispersed indicators, which is why the logic of the <1>Quantified Self</1> tends to decompose the self into data until meaning itself is emptied <2>Han</2><3>(Han, 2017, [p. 50])</3>. The point is to describe a kind of instability that is not born of subjective introspection, but of the replacement of narrative continuity by measurable tracking, making the maintenance of the self depend on indicators, goals and feedback that can be continuously recalibrated by external criteria.

<1>p. 358</1> The picture thickens when the record ceases to be individual memory and starts circulating as a criterion of validation, since tracking turns into self-surveillance and connects self-exploitation, self-observation and reputation maintenance. Han states that the digitized and networked subject carries an inner panopticon, in which guard and prisoner merge, so that control ceases to depend only on an exterior gaze and comes to operate as self-surveillance <2>Han</2><3>(Han, 2017, [p. 51])</3>. The consequence is that continuous evaluation ceases to be only the gaze of the environment and becomes an internalized gaze, turning self-adjustment into an ordinary requirement of permanence under metrics of performance and exposure that the subject himself helps to produce and to feed.

When experience comes to be organized by continuous measurement and comparison, conformity ceases to depend on explicit command and settles in as an ordinary effect of an environment that rewards predictability. Transparency operated by metrics and correlations does not function only as an expansion of available information, since it turns statistical patterns into a practical reference of normality, narrowing the space for deviation and shifting the cost of misalignment onto the very possibility of remaining visible and validated. In the IOC regime, this narrowing has a direct economic consequence, because the position of enjoyment depends on remaining commensurable and recognizable within the ecosystem, and the infrastructure controls the indicators and filters that define what will appear as adequate performance. The result is a regime of self-adjustment in which the maintenance of belonging and of positional value becomes dependent on adhering to measurable parameters that the environment measures and rewards, converting measurability into an instrument of governance.

The institutionally relevant effect of this picture can be described as identity captivity. The expression does not designate physical imprisonment nor assume an inability to act, but names a practical dependence, by which the continuity of enjoyment and the stability of symbolic identity come to be mediated by the administered ecosystem. When the position of enjoyment is anchored in signals of prestige, accumulated repertoires, performance records, visibility and belonging, the platform governs the conditions for preserving a socially recognizable place by distributing public legibility through metrics, ranking and internal eligibility criteria. In this context, leaving, slowing down or misaligning does not appear as a simple neutral choice, since it tends to imply loss of legibility and the collapse of the signals that sustain public commensurability, with downgrading of the position that gave economic meaning to enjoyment. Permanence comes to depend on continuous alignment with mutable operational <1>p. 359</1> standards, and leaving ceases to be a simple substitution of service, because it involves discontinuity of prestige, comparability and belonging.

This dependence on administered recognition is legally relevant because it makes integrity and identity governed variables of enjoyment and demands, at the dogmatic level, reinforced duties of qualified transparency, contestability, auditability and restoration proportional to the kind of power exercised by the <1>Lex Plataformae.  </1>

Dependence is consolidated because the platform concentrates the administration of metrics, recognition criteria and exposure trajectories, while freely recalibrating what counts as adequate performance and which conduct will be rewardable or punishable. The result is an exit cost that is not exhausted in a one-off patrimonial loss, since it involves the discontinuity of a narrative of self that was built, measured and validated inside the environment, besides loss of access to the very parameters that made this narrative intelligible. Identity captivity, thus, is the form in which the power of governance translates into stable subjection without ostensive coercion, because preserving enjoyment requires permanence under variable criteria and preserving symbolic identity requires continuity of recognition under signals that do not belong to the consumer, but to the infrastructure that defines and distributes them.

The exit barrier can be described as a form of social death inside the ecosystem. The expression does not operate as moral dramatization, but as a functional description of the effect produced when the platform concentrates the records that sustain belonging and relevance, that is, history, repertoire, ranked position, signals of prestige, community ties and traces of participation. Leaving the environment, under these conditions, is not like migrating from one service to another, because it implies interrupting one's very socially recognizable existence in that world, with loss of symbolic continuity and the practical erasure of trajectory marks that have become a condition of public commensurability. Leaving, therefore, does not present itself as a neutral consumption decision, since the cost is not limited to the price paid or to access to a utility, reaching the positional survival of the consumer in a grammar of recognition that the ecosystem itself monopolizes.

This effect stabilizes identity captivity through an additional mechanism, which depends not on formal coercion or direct threat, but on reputational self-preservation. If the experiential value of the IOC is anchored in signals of status, consistency of performance, belonging and social memory, any criticism that endangers the legitimacy of the ecosystem or the stability of its hierarchies tends to be perceived as a threat to the consumer's own identity investment. A circuit of defense of the environment is thus formed <1>p. 360</1> in which users become agents of conformity, not out of servility, but out of the need to protect the accumulated symbolic capital and the sense of social existence that derives from it. The platform, by organizing recognition as a scarce resource and conditioning its distribution on metrics and internal rules, produces a structural incentive for the community itself to operate as an instance of surveillance and containment of dissent, raising the social cost of misalignment and reducing the space for effective contestation.

What makes this regime particularly stable is that its machinery does not depend on continuous external coercion, since it operates through the exploitation of freedom as an economic resource. Byung-Chul Han states that neoliberalism constitutes a highly efficient system for exploiting freedom and capturing practices and expressive forms associated with autonomy, such as emotion, play and communication, arguing that exploiting people against their will is inefficient and that returns are maximized when freedom itself is exploited<1><2>389</2></1> <3>Han</3><4>(Han, 2017, [p. 9-10])</4>. The governed environment need not impose itself as prohibition to obtain adherence, since it encourages, rewards and makes engagement a condition of permanence, converting initiative and participation into the raw material of conformity.

This efficiency deepens when exploitation ceases to present itself as a visible relationship between dominator and dominated and comes to be internalized as an ordinary dynamic of the subject with himself. Han describes that, in the present, each individual tends to become a <1>p. 361</1> self-exploiting worker in his own enterprise, accumulating in the same figure the positions of command and submission, and that even class struggle can be lived as an inner struggle against oneself, under conditions defined by the solitude of the isolated, self-combative entrepreneur, who practices self-exploitation voluntarily <2>Han</2><3>(Han, 2017, [p. 11])</3>. The structural effect is the neutralization of frictions that, in other regimes, would make social conflict more visible and contestable, because the pressure is lived as an intimate obligation of performance and not as an external imposition attributable to an identifiable agent.

The operational language of this process appears in the transformation of life into a regime of measurable optimization, in which weaknesses and errors must be eliminated to maximize efficiency and performance, and in which everything is made to be comparable and measurable under the logic of quantifying success in the market, not in pursuit of the good life, but because of systemic constraints <1>Han</1><2>(Han, 2017, [p. 28])</2>. The triad composes the machinery of conformity in platform ecosystems: freedom is summoned as participation, participation is captured as productivity, and productivity is stabilized as comparability, so that the subject adjusts himself to remain rewardable and recognizable. The user becomes a practical agent of his own subjection within an environment in which a third party - not bound to any effective standards of transparency - administers metrics, visibility and permanence as “legitimate” conditions of value.

The result matters legally because it shifts the conflict from the vocabulary of choice to the plane of the governance conditions that produce, calibrate and make economically relevant what presents itself as choice. In IOC regimes, the permanence of value depends on recognition and continuity of enjoyment, and these elements do not stem from the isolated will of the consumer, since they are administered by criteria of visibility, comparison and sanction that the platform defines, applies and recalibrates. The subjection described, therefore, is not a moral trait nor an individual pathology, but a foreseeable effect of an environment in which performance, exposure and measurability function as a grammar of permanence. When the continuity of enjoyment requires self-adjustment and when the cost of misalignment manifests itself as loss of position, legibility and belonging, the environment comes to operate as a mechanism that produces vulnerability, because it transforms symbolic and positional risk into an instrument of conformity.

This shift prevents the problem from being treated as a simple informational asymmetry correctable by formal notice, or as a neutral competitive dynamic resolved by a market alternative. The platform concentrates the administration of the variables that define what will be recognized, rewarded, downgraded and excluded, and this concentration makes exploitable <1>p. 362</1> the consumer's dependence on parameters he does not control and that, as a rule, he cannot verify. Thus, protection cannot be limited to inventorying clauses or to presuming that the user's choice exhausts the meaning of the supply, because the effective shaping of the object is produced by continued operations of the ecosystem that determine conditions of access, permanence, reputation and sanction. The point reached is that vulnerability, in this scenario, has institutional density and demands duties proportional to the power exercised, especially regarding the intelligibility of criteria, the minimum stability of the conditions of enjoyment and the possibility of restoration when changes, modulations or sanctions degrade the position of enjoyment that gives economic meaning to the IOC.

The cost of this permanence through continuous recalibration appears more clearly when the temporality of the environment is described as game temporality, that is, organized by immediate rewards, short cycles of validation and quick experiences of success. Han observes that games exhibit a temporality marked by immediate success and reward, but that what matures over time cannot be gamified, because what is long and lasting tends to prove incompatible with the temporality of the game, so that hunting fits the regime of rewards, while farming, dependent on slow processes and quiet growth, does not let itself be converted into scores and levels, since life cannot be reduced to permanent hunting<1><2>390</2></1> <3>Han</3><4>(Han, 2017, [p. 43])</4>. Thus, it becomes possible to argue that the an ecosystem structured by comparison, performance and quick <5>feedback</5> tends to corrode the conditions of subjective continuity and experiential stability, demanding from the consumer incessant adjustment merely to remain legible and rewardable within the circuit that sustains the value of his IOC.

In this register, optimization ceases to function as a promise of improvement and comes to operate as a systemic requirement of permanence, since the environment values what can be intensified, measured and compared, pushing the subject toward a compulsion of <1>p. 363</1> productivity that admits no interruption. Han's formulations, although purposely loaded, help to fix the point in a technically useful way, since they describe a dynamic in which the positivity of performance converts inner life into fuel for the demand to produce more, and in which the very idea of adjustment shifts from care to exhaustion.

In ecosystems that administer recognition and permanence as conditions of value, the demand to remain in the game through continuous recalibration ceases to be individual discomfort and becomes a regular mechanism of governance, because enjoyment is maintained only while the subject manages to sustain, repeatedly, signals of adherence to the criteria of the environment.

The subjection described is not a side element of the IOC regime, because it indicates objectively the practical traction that allows private rules and technical sanctions to operate efficiently in the everyday life of ecosystems. When permanence depends on recognition, when continuity of enjoyment depends on adherence to metrics and when the cost of misalignment manifests itself as loss of position and social legibility, the subject is already invested in the environment even before the explicit act of <1>enforcement</1>.

In this scenario, the internal norm is not limited to declaring permissions and prohibitions, since it bears on a user who needs to remain rewardable and traceable, so that discipline is realized through the expectation of visibility, the risk of downgrading and the fear of functional exclusion, without depending on frontal coercion to stabilize conformity. The consequence is that governance by architecture and by information, by producing identity captivity, prepares the ground on which the private rule becomes effectively normative, because it finds a subject willing to adjust continuously to preserve what gives economic and existential meaning to his own IOC.

It is therefore necessary that the analysis advance from subjection to the normativity of the environment. Internal rules and technical <1>enforcement</1> do not operate only as contractual text, but as decisions implemented in filters, parameters, blocks, gradations and procedures that reconfigure enjoyment in real time. Once it is shown that adherence and self-adjustment are structural effects of the ecosystem, it becomes necessary to examine how internal policies are converted into effective restrictions and authorizations, with enough unilaterality and opacity to produce exclusion and functional dispossession. The next step, therefore, consists in describing the <2>Lex Plataformae</2> and its <3>enforcement</3> as the practical normativity of the environment, since it is at this level that private power becomes legally controllable in proportional terms.

In the work <1>Psychopolitics: Neoliberalism and New Technologies of Power</1>, originally entitled <2>Psychopolitik</2>., the South Korean philosopher based in Germany, Byung-Chul Han <3>(2017)</3>, proposes a reading of contemporary forms of power based on the shift from external coercion to mechanisms of internalized exploitation. The book argues that, under neoliberal rationality and technological mediation, freedom, initiative and performance cease to operate as emancipatory promises and come to function as instruments of self-binding, in which the subject governs himself through optimization, transparency and productivity. The usefulness is descriptive. The categories proposed by Han allow naming how information technologies, metrics and regimes of visibility convert adherence, self-adjustment and continuous comparison into stable conformity, above all in environments in which recognition and permanence become conditions of value. In <4>Sociedade do Cansaço </4> (2015), originally entitled <5>Müdigkeitsgesellschaft</5>, Han presents a convergent diagnosis from another entry point: the passage from a model of discipline centered on negativity, prohibition and the external enemy to a regime of positivity in which the imperative of performance imposes itself as self-demand. The text describes the replacement of the obedience-subject by the achievement-subject, whose exploitation does not depend on frontal coercion because it is realized as self-exploitation and the inability to interrupt the logic of continuous optimization. The work offers useful language to describe how environments structured by comparison, goals, rewards and continuous visibility can produce subjection through excess and self-adjustment, without individualizing psychologization, allowing conformity to be treated as a structural effect of an ecosystem that administers symbolic risk and distributes recognition as a scarce resource. <6>↩</6>

In the article <1>What’s Next for Ranked</1>, Riot presents structural changes to the ladder as management of distribution and progression, treating the system as an object of regular adjustments, with a revision of promos and the introduction of a new tier (“the introduction of a new Ranked tier”) <2>Riot Games</2><3>(Riot Games, 2023d)</3>. The text is valuable for the vignette because it shows, in institutional language, that the ladder is administered as an infrastructure of trajectory and belonging, and not as a simple neutral scoreboard. When the platform alters how one climbs, how one is distributed and how the subject's position is qualified, it redefines what counts as sufficient performance and repositions the relative value of the consumer within the ecosystem, reinforcing the logic of continuous self-adjustment that characterizes the psychopolitics of performance. <4>↩</4>

The contract records that, if the account is terminated, the user “will no longer have access to your account, including associated data or Virtual Content” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>.It also provides that access to the services operates as a “limited, non-exclusive, non-transferable and revocable license”, “expressly conditioned” on the terms of the contract, and that termination automatically cancels this license <3>Riot Games</3><4>(Riot Games, 2024e)</4>.It is inferred, therefore, that the ranked position and its public legibility do not constitute an autonomous “good”, but an institutional effect maintained under conditions of administered access, which reinforces the reading of the exit cost as loss of intelligibility and commensurability inside the environment. <5>↩</5>

In the official Honor guide, Riot states that the system “is a general reflection of any player's behavior in and out of game” and that it “rewards sportsmanlike conduct” while it “penalizes inappropriate behavior” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2025a)</2>.The same page describes the coupling between conduct and practical effects by indicating that Honor offers “additional benefits” and, conversely, involves “limited communication privileges” and reduced rewards <3>Riot Games</3><4>(Riot Games, 2025a)</4>.The value lies in making explicit in institutional language what the theoretical text already describes: a discipline that operates as an incentive to adequate participation and as a functional cost of misalignment, producing self-management of conduct to preserve eligibility and permanence. <5>↩</5>

In this sense, Honor is described by the community as a system with levels and <1>checkpoints</1> in which levels 1 and 0 are “restricted Honor levels obtainable only through penalties” and “carry far fewer rewards than the normal levels” <2>League of Legends Wiki</2><3>(League of Legends Wiki, [202-?]a)</3>. The same entry indicates that punished individuals “will get demoted in Honor level” and that, in cases of chat restriction, there is demotion to “level 1, or 0 if already at level 1”, establishing a logic of fall associated with sanction and a progression fragmented by <4>checkpoints</4>. The description successfully compiles the grammar of levels, <5>checkpoints</5> and rewards, allowing governance by eligibility to be characterized precisely. <6>↩</6>

In the Terms, Riot makes explicit that the user agrees to follow the “User Rules”, which “govern behavior during the game” and also “certain conduct outside the game”, and adds that Clause 7 “explains the penalties”, including “temporary suspensions”, “suspension or termination of the account and its deletion” and “hardware banning” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>.What matters here is the way discipline is integrated into the contractual bond as an ordinary possibility of modulating access, with enough intensity to convert eligibility into a permanent concern of the user. <3>↩</3>

The contract states that the User Rules “apply not only within our Services, but also while you stream on a streaming platform”, and adds that they “also apply to your recorded videos and social media posts” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>.In addition, it records that “misconduct in one of our games may result in penalties applicable in another game” and admits “temporary or permanent bans and account suspensions applicable to all of our games” <3>Riot Games</3><4>(Riot Games, 2024e)</4>. Therefore, the normativity of the environment is not reduced to an internal prohibition of the “match”, since it operates as extended governance, affecting the company's ecosystem as a a whole, including its other games, in terms of conduct and identity, with practical effects on access and permanence that feed and potentializes the internalization of control. <5>↩</5>

“As the entrepreneur of its own self, the neoliberal subject has no capacity for relationships with others that might be free of purpose. Nor do entrepreneurs know what purpose-free friendship would even look like. Originally, being free meant being among friends. ‘Freedom’ and ‘friendship’ have the same root in Indo-European languages. Fundamentally, freedom signifies a relationship. A real feeling of freedom occurs only in a fruitful relationship - when being with others brings happiness. But today’s neoliberal regime leads to utter isolation; as such, it does not really free us at all. Accordingly, the question now is whether we need to redefine freedom - to reinvent it - in order to escape from the fatal dialectic that is changing freedom into coercion. Neoliberalism represents a highly efficient, indeed an intelligent, system for exploiting freedom. Everything that belongs to practices and expressive forms of liberty - emotion, play and communication - comes to be exploited. It is inefficient to exploit people against their will. Allo-exploitation yields scant returns. Only when freedom is exploited are returns maximized. It is interesting to note that Marx also defines freedom in terms of a successful relationship to others: ‘Only in community [with others does each] individual [have] the means of cultivating his gifts in all directions; only in the community, therefore, is personal freedom possible.’1 From this perspective, being free means nothing other than self-realization with others. Freedom is synonymous with a working community (i.e., a successful one). For Marx, individual freedom represents a ruse - a trick of capital. ‘Free competition’, which is based on the idea of individual freedom, simply amounts to the ‘relation of capital to itself as another capital, i.e., the real conduct of capital as capital’. Capital reproduces by entering into relations with itself as another form of Capital: through free competition. It copulates with the Other of itself by way of individual freedom. Capital grows inasmuch as people engage in free competition. Hereby, individual freedom amounts to servitude inasmuch as Capital lays hold of it and uses it for its own propagation. That is, Capital exploits individual freedom in order to breed: ‘It is not the individuals who are set free by free competition; it is, rather, capital which is set free.’ The freedom of Capital achieves self-realization by way of individual freedom. In the process, individuals degrade into the genital organs of Capital. Individual freedom lends it an ‘automatic’ subjectivity of its own, which spurs it to reproduce actively. In this way, Capital continuously ‘brings forth living offspring’. Today, individual freedom is taking on excessive forms; ultimately, this amounts to nothing other than the excess of Capital itself.“ <1>Han</1><2>(Han, 2017, [p. 9-10], emphasis in the original)</2> <3>↩</3>

“In order to heighten productivity, emotional capitalism also enlists playing and games - which should, in fact, be the Other of Work, its opposite. Emotional capitalism is gamifying the life- and working world. Playing games lends an emotional, indeed a dramatic, charge to working - which in turn generates more motivation. Because games rapidly deliver a sense of success and reward, the result is higher performance and a greater yield. A person playing a game, being emotionally invested, is much more engaged than a worker who acts rationally or is simply functioning. Games exhibit a specific temporality marked by immediate experiences of success and reward. But what matures over time cannot be gamified. Whatever is long, anything that lasts a long time, proves incompatible with the game’s temporality. Hunting, for instance, matches the mode of the game, whereas farming, which depends on slow processes of ripening and quiet growth, cannot be gamified at all. Life cannot be turned into hunting alone. The gamification of work exploits homo ludens. The player subjugates him- or herself to the order of domination in the very act of playing. Today, the gamification logic of ‘Likes’, ‘Friends’ and ‘Followers’ means that social communication is also being plugged into and subordinated to a game mode. The corollary of the gamification of communication is its commercialization. That said, this process is destroying human communication.” <1>Han</1><2>(Han, 2017, [p. 43], emphasis in the original)</2>. <3>↩</3>
